passage: Urmila's scooter was stolen, so she went to the police station with the registration papers and a photo of the bike, spoke respectfully and asked for a stamped paper showing what she had reported, which the constable handed over. The next month a traffic officer fined her for something she had not done, and she felt furious and helpless. She wanted to shout, but she noted the receipt number and the time and filed a complaint on the official portal with help from her aunt Usha. Around then her friend Danish phoned late. "If they ask, say I was with you on Friday night." Urmila's stomach turned. "I won't lie to the police. But I'll come with you to see a lawyer and help you sort it out properly." Danish grumbled but went. Later, an officer at a checkpoint said she could pay him some cash and forget the paperwork, and pushed a paper toward her to sign. She said politely, "I haven't read this. I'd like my aunt to be here," and wrote down his name and badge number. Her roommate Hafsa sat with her that night and helped her report it.

qa.q: What did Urmila bring to the police station?
qa.a: She brought the registration papers and a photo of the bike.

qa.q: How did Urmila's report of the theft differ from what happened at the checkpoint?
qa.a: At the station she brought papers, stayed respectful and got a stamped paper showing her report; at the checkpoint the officer asked for cash and pushed a paper to sign, so she refused to sign what she had not read, asked for her aunt and noted his name and badge number.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling after the unfair fine?
qa.a: She felt furious and helpless, but she chose to record the details instead of shouting.

qa.q: What did Urmila offer Danish instead of lying for him?
qa.a: She offered to go with him to see a lawyer, showing loyalty without giving a false statement.

grounding: One young adult meets the police as a trusting complainant, an angry recipient of an unfair fine, a loyal friend asked to lie and a person pressed for money and a signature.
